evidence.quote: The route travels through mostly unoccupied desert terrain, with much of its alignment paralleling the northern edges of the Nellis Air Force Range.

evidence.quote: The highway stretches from State Route 318 at Crystal Springs northwest to U.S. Route 6 (US 6) at Warm Springs.

evidence.claim: It remains lightly traveled.
evidence.quote: SR 375 remains a lightly traveled route.

evidence.claim: The state named it the Extraterrestrial Highway in 1996 after travelers reported UFOs near Area 51; the Nevada Commission on Tourism sought the name to attract visitors.
evidence.quote: To capitalize on the purported paranormal activity along the route, the Nevada Commission on Tourism sought to rename the highway. State officials drew inspiration from the alien legends and dubbed SR 375 the Extraterrestrial Highway in February 1996.

evidence.claim: The road’s earlier changes came from military restrictions.
evidence.quote: To avoid the restricted area of the testing range, the west end of SR 25 was realigned by 1957.

evidence.claim: An unimproved route existed by 1932 as SR 25A, becoming part of SR 25 the next year.
evidence.quote: An unimproved road approximating the present alignment of State Route 375 came into existence by 1932. This route, christened State Route 25A

evidence.claim: An unimproved route existed by 1932 as SR 25A, becoming part of SR 25 the next year.
evidence.quote: By 1933, SR 25A had been renumbered to become a new western segment of State Route 25.

evidence.claim: By 1957 its western end had shifted to Warm Springs to avoid the testing range, taking the road north of the Reveille Range instead of across the Kawich Range.
evidence.quote: To avoid the restricted area of the testing range, the west end of SR 25 was realigned by 1957. The highway connected to US 6 at Warm Springs about 37 miles (60 km) east of the previous terminus, heading north around the Reveille Range instead of climbing the Kawich Range within the bombing area.

evidence.claim: Paving was complete the following year.
evidence.quote: The entire highway was paved by the following year.

evidence.claim: Nevada’s 1976 highway renumbering made this western section SR 375, a number first printed on the official state highway map in 1978.
evidence.quote: SR 25 remained unchanged until the 1976 renumbering of Nevada's state highways, through which the western section of SR 25 became the new State Route 375. The new route number was first seen on the 1978 edition of the official state highway map.

evidence.claim: From US 6 at Warm Springs, follow the base of the Reveille Range into Railroad Valley, then climb Queen City Summit, the road’s highest point at 5,935 feet.
evidence.quote: The route climbs out of Sand Spring Valley and heads over the 5,935-foot (1,809 m) Queen City Summit, the highest point on the highway. After passing the summit, the route descends into the southern end of Railroad Valley, curving nearly due north for several miles as it follows the base of Reveille Range.

evidence.claim: Descend into Sand Spring Valley and Rachel, then cross Coyote Summit toward Tikaboo Valley and Mail Box Road.
evidence.quote: West of the summit, the Extraterrestrial Highway descends into the Sand Spring Valley and the community of Rachel becomes visible.

evidence.claim: Descend into Sand Spring Valley and Rachel, then cross Coyote Summit toward Tikaboo Valley and Mail Box Road.
evidence.quote: As the highway heads northwest through Tikaboo Valley, it meets Mail Box Road.

evidence.claim: Descend into Sand Spring Valley and Rachel, then cross Coyote Summit toward Tikaboo Valley and Mail Box Road.
evidence.quote: SR 375 continues heading northwest from the mailbox, climbing in elevation again to reach the top of Coyote Summit

evidence.claim: Hancock Summit is the last crossing before the route ends at SR 318 in Crystal Springs.
evidence.quote: State Route 375 begins at a "Y" junction with State Route 318 at Crystal Springs

evidence.claim: Hancock Summit is the last crossing before the route ends at SR 318 in Crystal Springs.
evidence.quote: From Crystal Springs, the highway curves southwest to pass between the Pahrangat and Mount Irish ranges to ascend 5,592-foot (1,704 m) Hancock Summit.

evidence.claim: Rachel’s time capsule came from the producers of Independence Day in 1996 and is intended to be opened in 2050.
evidence.quote: In 1996, the producers of the movie Independence Day gave the town a time capsule, which is installed near the inn and is intended to be opened in 2050.

evidence.claim: That April, film stars joined state officials in town for the highway’s public dedication.
evidence.quote: A public dedication ceremony for the Extraterrestrial Highway was held in Rachel in April 1996. State dignitaries at the ceremony were joined by studio executives and Independence Day stars

evidence.claim: The town began in 1973, founded by alfalfa farmer D.C. Day, and was first called Tempiute Village, then Sand Springs.
evidence.quote: Rachel was founded in May 1973 by a local alfalfa farmer named D.C. Day. The community was first known as Tempiute Village, and then later as Sand Springs.

evidence.claim: In 1978 it took the name of Rachel Jones, the first baby born in the valley.
evidence.quote: On February 15, 1978, the town was renamed to Rachel after the first baby born in the valley, Rachel Jones (1978–1980).

evidence.claim: When Rachel Jones died in 1980, residents created a cemetery and memorial park in her memory.
evidence.quote: Rachel Jones died on May 24, 1980. In memory of her, Rachel residents created a cemetery and memorial park.

evidence.claim: The capsule is installed near the Little A’Le’Inn.
evidence.quote: a small bar, restaurant and motel located in Rachel

evidence.claim: The capsule is installed near the Little A’Le’Inn.

evidence.claim: The Black Mailbox kept its name even after its color changed.
evidence.quote: The original mailbox was a normal black mailbox; however, due to people constantly sifting through it, it was replaced by a more secure white mailbox. The name "Black Mailbox" still stuck.

evidence.claim: It marked Mail Box Road, a dirt route from SR 375 toward restricted land surrounding Area 51.
evidence.quote: It used to be marked by a single postal drop known as the "black mailbox": the dirt access road leads to the restricted lands surrounding Area 51.

evidence.claim: People searching through the original mailbox prompted its replacement with a more secure white one.
evidence.quote: due to people constantly sifting through it, it was replaced by a more secure white mailbox.

evidence.claim: The spot became a gathering place for UFO seekers, but owner Steve Medlin removed the mailbox because of continued vandalism.
evidence.quote: It was commonly used as a gathering place for UFO seekers

evidence.claim: The spot became a gathering place for UFO seekers, but owner Steve Medlin removed the mailbox because of continued vandalism.
evidence.quote: The mailbox was removed by its owner, Steve Medlin, due to continued vandalism.

evidence.quote: the dirt access road leads to the restricted lands surrounding Area 51.

evidence.claim: A junction and a few trees mark Crystal Springs at the southeastern end of SR 375.
evidence.quote: The site, which is little more than the junction and a few trees, functions as a rest area.

evidence.claim: The ghost town stands where SR 375 meets SR 318, northwest of US 93.
evidence.quote: The ghost town is located at the junction of State Route 318 and State Route 375 (Extraterrestrial Highway), just northwest of U.S. Route 93.

evidence.claim: Silver ore discovered here in 1865 led to its becoming Lincoln County’s first seat, from 1866 to 1867, before Hiko replaced it.
evidence.quote: In 1865, Crystal Springs was the first area in Lincoln County where mining grade silver ore was discovered.  This led to Crystal Springs becoming the first county seat of Lincoln County from 1866 to 1867, although it was later replaced by Hiko.

evidence.claim: Nearby springs and marshes along the White River supply irrigation to ranches and farms.
evidence.quote: it is a large group of marshes and springs along the White River. Crystal Springs provides irrigation for multiple nearby ranches and farms

evidence.claim: Nevada Historical Marker 205 identifies the ghost town.
evidence.quote: The ghost town is marked as Nevada Historical Marker 205 (Crystal Springs).

evidence.claim: The nearby springs also supplied water to people traveling the Mormon Trail through this part of Nevada.
evidence.quote: The springs provided water for people traveling the Mormon Trail.

flags: The cache establishes an official highway name, not Nevada Scenic Byway program membership. Catalog designation needs correction.
The southeastern terminus is SR 318 at Crystal Springs, not US 93 as material states.
All cached sources are secondary. Road naming, realignment and the restricted-land note lack cached agency corroboration. Checked date records cache review, not a live access check.
Mail Box Road is shorter than 90 words. Do not promise a mailbox is currently present; the cached account records removal and provides no verified replacement.
No substantive claim from current was wholly unsupported. Omitted the current population estimate and rounded route mileage; the preserved landmarks and historical claims have cache support.
